patient.name: Gregory Alston
patient.chiefComplaint: Sudden severe headache with vomiting and declining responsiveness

history.hpi: Coworker reports the patient suddenly grabbed his head, described it as "the worst headache of my life," and vomited twice within minutes. Over the next several minutes he became progressively less responsive, now only groaning to voice.
medications: Lisinopril 20 mg PO daily (per coworker, inconsistent compliance)
history.lastOralIntake: Coffee approximately 1 hour prior to onset
history.events: Coworker witnessed sudden onset at the office; called 911 immediately when the patient began vomiting and became less responsive

scene.dispatch: 58-year-old male, severe headache, now less responsive, office building
scene.location: Office break room, patient on the floor beside an overturned chair
scene.bystanders: Coworker present, witnessed sudden onset and progressive decline in responsiveness
visualCues: Patient supine on floor, emesis visible nearby
Patient groaning, eyes closed, not following commands
Coworker anxiously relaying the timeline of events

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 58-year-old male with a witnessed sudden-onset severe headache, vomiting, and rapidly declining level of consciousness, now responsive only to voice with groaning.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but at risk given vomiting and declining mentation
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Left pupil sluggish and slightly larger than right
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Withdraws to voice, no clear focal weakness distinguishable at this time
otherFindings: Neck stiffness noted on gentle exam

transitions.if: Stroke scale, BGL, and LKW established
transitions.condition: Crew performs a validated stroke scale, checks blood glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a mimic, and establishes a precise last-known-well time from the coworker while continuously monitoring for airway compromise.

phases.name: Stroke scale, BGL, and LKW established
phases.description: Crew completes a validated stroke scale, checks blood glucose to exclude a mimic, and documents the witnessed last-known-well time, while closely monitoring the patient's rapidly declining level of consciousness and vomiting for signs of impending airway compromise.
phases.triggerCondition: The crew completes a validated stroke scale, confirms normal blood glucose, and documents last known well from the coworker's witnessed account, all while the patient's level of consciousness continues to trend downward.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but increasingly at risk; gag reflex sluggish
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Left pupil now more dilated and sluggish than right
otherFindings: Bradycardic with widening pulse pressure (Cushing's triad developing)

expectedActions.shortAction: Perform validated prehospital stroke scale despite declining mentation; positive for asymmetric pupils and unresponsiveness
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Use a validated prehospital stroke scale that may include, but is not limited to: Facial smile/grimace, Arm drift, Speech
expectedActions.rationale: A validated scale still drives destination and pre-notification decisions even in a severely affected patient.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check blood glucose to rule out hypoglycemia as a mimic (result 108 mg/dL, no treatment needed)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check blood glucose level (BGL). Treat only if glucose less than 60 mg/dL
expectedActions.rationale: Hypoglycemia is a rapidly reversible cause of AMS that must be excluded.

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish witnessed last-known-well time from coworker
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Determine "last known well" time. History – "last known well" and source of that information
expectedActions.rationale: LKW time is essential documentation even when the primary concern shifts to airway management.

transitions.condition: With GCS now 9 and loss of protective airway reflexes plus active vomiting, the crew proceeds with rapid sequence intubation to protect the airway before further decline.
The crew continues focusing on the stroke workup without escalating airway management despite the patient's declining GCS, sluggish gag reflex, and active vomiting.

phases.name: RSI performed for airway protection
phases.description: Recognizing loss of protective airway reflexes with active vomiting and a GCS of 9, the crew proceeds with rapid sequence intubation, suctioning the soiled airway first and pre-oxygenating before the procedure.
phases.triggerCondition: With GCS 9, a sluggish gag reflex, and ongoing emesis risking aspiration, the crew suctions the airway, preoxygenates, and performs RSI to secure a definitive airway.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Ventilated via BVM, chest rise symmetric
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Left pupil fixed and dilated, right sluggish
otherFindings: Airway suctioned of emesis prior to intubation
Endotracheal tube placed and confirmed with waveform capnography

expectedActions.shortAction: Suction soiled airway prior to intubation attempt
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Suction airway: for significantly contaminated airways, consider utilizing a suction assisted laryngeal airway decontamination (SALAD) technique. Suctioning to limit aspiration is a priority
expectedActions.rationale: Active vomiting must be cleared before airway instrumentation to limit aspiration risk.

expectedActions.shortAction: Fentanyl 90 mcg IV premedication (90 kg × 1 mcg/kg), 2-3 minutes prior to intubation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider pre-medication with Fentanyl, 1 mcg/kg, 2-3 minutes prior to intubation attempt
expectedActions.rationale: Blunts the sympathetic/ICP response to laryngoscopy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Etomidate 22.5 mg IV push (90 kg × 0.25 mg/kg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer induction sedative agent: Etomidate IV push, 0.2-0.3 mg/kg
expectedActions.rationale: Etomidate provides hemodynamically stable induction, important given the elevated ICP and bradycardia already present.

expectedActions.shortAction: Rocuronium 90 mg IV push (90 kg × 1 mg/kg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer paralytic agent: Rocuronium IV push, 1 mg/kg
expectedActions.rationale: Provides paralysis for first-pass intubation success.

expectedActions.shortAction: Confirm tube placement with waveform capnography, bilateral breath sounds, and absent gastric sounds
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Confirm placement of advanced airway (endotracheal tube, SGA) with waveform capnography (most reliable), absent gastric sounds, and bilateral breath sounds
expectedActions.rationale: Waveform capnography is the most reliable confirmation method and must be checked before committing to the tube.

transitions.if: Tube secured, ventilation continued to transport
transitions.condition: Tube is confirmed and secured; crew continues manual ventilation with continuous waveform capnography monitoring en route to a comprehensive stroke center.

phases.name: Tube secured, ventilation continued to transport
phases.description: With the airway secured, the crew continues manual ventilation targeting an EtCO2 of 35-45 mmHg, continuously monitors tube placement, and transports emergently to a comprehensive stroke center capable of neurosurgical intervention.
phases.triggerCondition: After confirming tube placement, the crew ventilates at a normal rate and volume targeting EtCO2 35-45 mmHg (reserving mild hyperventilation only for overt herniation signs), and transports emergently.

clinicalPresentation.pupils: Left pupil fixed and dilated, right sluggish
otherFindings: Tube position reassessed after each patient movement

expectedActions.shortAction: Ventilate to maintain EtCO2 35-45 mmHg; reserve mild hyperventilation for overt herniation signs only
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: In patients without primary pulmonary pathology ... maintain EtCO2 of no less than 35 and up to 40 mmHg. In patients with severe head injury with signs of herniation (unilateral dilated pupil or decerebrate posturing), modest hyperventilation to EtCO2 no less than 30 mmHg may be considered for a brief time
expectedActions.rationale: Routine hyperventilation is harmful; it is reserved only for overt herniation signs, and even then only briefly.

phases.name: Airway protection delayed
phases.description: The crew continues the stroke workup without escalating airway management despite a declining GCS and active vomiting. The patient's gag reflex is lost and emesis is aspirated, causing acute desaturation.
phases.triggerCondition: Airway management is not escalated despite GCS falling to 9 with active vomiting; the patient aspirates and desaturates acutely.

clinicalPresentation.pupils: Left pupil fixed and dilated, right sluggish

expectedActions.shortAction: Emergently suction airway, then proceed to RSI without further delay
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Suctioning to limit aspiration is a priority, since it is associated with development of hospital acquired pneumonia and related increases in ICU stay and mortality. Altered mental status with loss of normal protective airway reflexes
expectedActions.rationale: Once aspiration occurs, immediate suctioning and definitive airway placement are required to prevent further hypoxic injury.
